drills.q: Explain the three Log Analytics log tiers and the real tradeoff each represents.
drills.a: Analytics Logs (~$2.30/GB) support full KQL: joins, summarize, indexing, alerting. Basic Logs (~$0.50/GB) drop joins/summarize entirely, usable for filter-and-view access to high-volume rarely-aggregated data. Auxiliary Logs (~$0.05/GB) target compliance data queryable only via an async search job. Tiers are configured per-table, not workspace-wide.

drills.q: A KQL query against a high-volume security log table times out. Diagnose the likely structural issue.
drills.a: The 'where' filter is likely applied after an expensive join/summarize, or an early selective filter (like a specific EventID) is missing -- an unfiltered 24-hour query against a table like SecurityEvent can scan 50-500 million rows. Fix: restructure so the most selective where clause runs first, before any join or aggregation.

drills.q: A team reports 'missing' distributed traces despite Application Insights being fully configured. What's the most likely explanation?
drills.a: Adaptive sampling (on by default) or fixed-rate sampling is working as designed -- not every request is traced. Confirm by checking configured sampling settings and observed sampled percentage rather than assuming an instrumentation bug.

drills.q: Why does setting an ingestion sampling rate in the Azure portal sometimes have no observable effect?
drills.a: When the Application Insights ingestion endpoint detects telemetry already arrived with a sampling rate below 100% (SDK-level adaptive or fixed-rate sampling active), it ignores any configured ingestion sampling rate entirely -- SDK-level sampling takes precedence over ingestion-point sampling.

drills.q: Estimate the daily span-ingestion cost for a service at 100 RPS, 10 spans/request, full unsampled tracing, and explain why this matters.
drills.a: 100 x 10 x 86,400s = ~86 million spans/day. At ~$0.50-2.50 per million spans typical vendor tracing rate, that's roughly $43-215/day for ONE service. This turns sampling from a noise-reduction choice into a direct, material cost-control decision, especially across a fleet of services.

drills.q: Compare Azure Cost Management to AWS Cost Explorer on the dimension most likely to matter for a large multi-team organization.
drills.a: Azure Cost Management is stronger for cross-subscription budget governance -- budgets scoped at the management-group level mirroring the RBAC hierarchy. AWS Cost Explorer is stronger on automated remediation actions and has a longer free historical lookback (12 months). For large multi-team Azure orgs, the management-group-aligned budget hierarchy is the more differentiating capability.

drills.q: Design a Log Analytics workspace topology for dev/staging/prod plus a 7-year compliance audit retention requirement.
drills.a: Separate workspaces per environment for isolation, using cross-workspace KQL union/workspace() queries for cross-cutting investigations. Active dashboards/alerts data stays on Analytics Logs with standard interactive retention. 7-year compliance audit data goes on Auxiliary Logs (cheapest ingestion) with Long-Term Retention (up to 12 years), accepting async search-job access instead of live KQL.

drills.q: A team's Log Analytics bill spikes after a new microservice's verbose debug logging goes to production. Fix without disabling logging.
drills.a: Check whether that log source is landing in the default Analytics Logs tier despite being high-volume and rarely aggregated. If it's mostly filtered/viewed rather than joined/summarized, route it to Basic Logs (~1/5 the cost), preserving debugging capability at lower cost. Must first audit existing queries/alerts against that table, since Basic Logs breaks any join/summarize dependency.

drills.q: Explain what a KQL summary rule does and the specific pattern it optimizes.
drills.a: Pre-aggregates high-volume raw data at ingestion time into a smaller target table, so a recurring query (detection/dashboard running every few minutes against a large table) hits the pre-aggregated table instead of re-scanning raw data each run -- reportedly cutting per-query compute by 90%+ for that 'same aggregation, run repeatedly' pattern. The raw table remains available for ad-hoc, row-level investigation.

drills.q: Why is KQL described as having no direct AWS/GCP equivalent, and what's the practical implication for an AWS-experienced engineer?
drills.a: CloudWatch Logs Insights and Cloud Logging share surface-level ideas but are different engines with different syntax and performance characteristics from KQL's pipe-based, Kusto-engine-specific model (shared across Log Analytics, App Insights, Sentinel, Fabric Real-Time Intelligence). Practical implication: budget real learning time for KQL's filter-before-aggregate discipline and join syntax -- it doesn't transfer automatically from CloudWatch Logs Insights fluency.

drills.q: Explain why Application Insights' shift to OpenTelemetry-based instrumentation matters architecturally.
drills.a: It replaces the older proprietary Application Insights SDK with the same vendor-neutral instrumentation standard AWS (X-Ray) and GCP (Cloud Trace) have adopted, closing a real portability gap -- instrumentation code becomes more reusable across backends rather than locking an application into Azure-specific tracing APIs.
